explanations.E0032:
# E0032: value of the wrong type

A value must have the type its position expects: the declared type of a `let`, the parameter of a function, the return type of a function, the operand of an operator.

## Why

Sisu does not convert between number types by itself. A `u8`, a `char`, an `i64` and an `f64` are different types even when the number would fit, so a program says where one becomes another with `u8(...)`, `i64(...)`, `f64(...)` or `char(...)`. A `u8` and a `char` convert through `i64`: `char(i64(b))`, and `f64(i64(b))`. A conversion takes one type: `i64(...)` takes a `u8`, a `char` or an `f64`, and `u8(...)`, `char(...)` and `f64(...)` take an `i64`. An `i64` beside an `f64` in arithmetic or a comparison, as in `n * x`, is the one reported, with the unsafe fix to convert it: `f64(n) * x`. Where the context wants an `i64`, as `n += x` does, the `f64` is the one reported, and no fix converts it. A value that does not fit makes `u8(...)` or `char(...)` fail, and an `f64` that is not a whole number in `i64`'s range makes `i64(...)` fail, so each gives an optional, a `u8?`, a `char?` or an `i64?`: give a default with `??`, or unwrap it with `if let`. The fix that converts is offered only where that optional is expected.

A value converts to an optional through one `?` only: `let x: i64? = 5` is valid, but `let x: i64?? = 5` is not. Wrap the value in `Some(...)` for each further layer: `let x: i64?? = Some(5)`.

A value converts to an interface value, `any Shape`, when its type conforms to `Shape` and it is not an optional. An `i64?` is no `any Display`, and a `Circle?` is no `any Shape` and no `(any Shape)?`. Unwrap the optional with `if let` or `??`, then convert the value. A `Circle` converts to `(any Shape)?` and is wrapped.

A `panic` or `todo` message is a `string`. An `i64`, `u8`, `f64`, `bool` or `char` written on one line becomes one with interpolation: `panic(n)` is `panic("{n}")`, and `todo(n)` is `todo("{n}")`.

A string's `get` takes a range written in the call, such as `s.get(1..3)`. An argument that is not a range, such as `s.get(1)`, is this error. An array's `get` takes an `i64`, so a range such as `xs.get(0..2)` is this error too. Write `xs[0..2]`, which stops the program when the range is out of bounds.

When it can, the report says where the required type comes from. The source can be a parameter, a return type, a `let` with a written type, a field, a payload or a constant. It can also be an assignment to a local name, an earlier `break`, an element or a branch. For a type parameter, it is the argument that gave the type. A secondary label marks the place in your code. When the place is in the prelude, a note says it instead. Some forms do not give the source yet. These include an operator, a pattern, a field, index or compound assignment, and a `while` condition or match guard. They also include the fallback of `??`, a `Some` value, and a field, payload or prelude parameter whose type is generic.

An `if` condition gets the label "a condition must be `bool`". An index of a place gets "an index must be `i64`". A value index on an array gets "an index must be `i64` or a range".

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let n: i64 = 5
    let b: u8 = n
    print(b)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let n: i64 = 5
    let b: u8 = u8(n) ?? 0
    print(b)
}
```
explanations.E0033:
# E0033: name that is not in scope

A name in an expression must be a binding in scope: a `let`, a parameter, or a binding made by `for`, `if let` or `while let`. A binding is in scope from its declaration to the end of its block.

The name of a type is no binding: `f64` or a class's name read as a value is [E0105](E0105.md). So is the name of a function read as a value.

When a binding in scope has a similar name, the error offers it as an unsafe fix. The unsafe fix may be wrong: the name could be a binding that was never declared.

## Why

Sisu does not resolve a misspelled name on its own. A misspelled name, or one used after its block has ended, would otherwise read some other value or none.

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let total = 3
    print(totl)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let total = 3
    print(total)
}
```
explanations.E0050:
# E0050: a type that cannot be inferred

`None` takes the optional type its position expects. Where nothing says which type, Sisu cannot choose one.

## Why

Every optional is an optional of some type: `None` of `i64?` and `None` of `Tree?` are different values. A `let` with no type has nothing to take it from.

The help of a `let` with `None` or `[]` writes the type from the first later use of the local that gives one. A use can be a call argument, a `return`, an assignment or a `push`. When no use gives a type, the help writes `...` in its place, as in `let x: ...? = None`.

A call of a generic function, class or variant has the same problem when nothing fixes one of its type parameters. `first([])` gives `T` no type: the `[]` has none of its own, and a later use of the result does not count. Annotate the result, `let x: i64? = first([])`, or write the type arguments, `first<i64>([])`. A parameter that the result names only through an associated type, as `S` in `-> [S.Item]`, is not fixed by an annotation of the result: write the type arguments, `collect<Countdown>()`.

An alias whose body does not use a type parameter has the same problem. In `type F<T> = f64`, no value gives `T` a type, so the compiler cannot infer `T` at `F.pi`. Write the type argument, `F<i64>.pi`, or remove `T` from the alias, `type F = f64`. Sisu gives no warning for a type parameter that nothing uses.

`Some(None)` has the same problem: `Some` holds a value of any type, and `None` has no type of its own. Annotate the optional, `let x: i64?? = Some(None)`.

`Ok(1)` has the same problem: `Ok` holds the value, and nothing says the type of the error. Annotate the result, `let r: Result<i64, string> = Ok(1)`. `Err("bad")` leaves the type of the value open in the same way.

`x ?? None ?? 0` has the same problem, because `??` groups to the right. It is `x ?? (None ?? 0)`, and nothing gives that `None` a type. To remove two layers from an `i64??`, write `(x ?? None) ?? 0`.

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x = None
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x: i64? = None
    print(x ?? 0)
}
```
explanations.E0094:
# E0094: arithmetic on `char`

The binary `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` and the compound assignments `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `%=` do not take a `char`, on either side. The sign `-c` is not arithmetic on a `char`: it is [E0032](E0032.md), as `c` is not an `i64`. A `char` is compared with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, by code point, and converted with `i64(c)`.

## Why

A `char` is a Unicode scalar value, not a number. Adding to it can land on a code point that is no `char`, in the gap `D800` to `DFFF` or past `10FFFF`. The program says where a `char` becomes a number and where it becomes a `char` again. `char(n)` gives a `char?`, which is `None` when `n` is not a scalar value, so the program also says what to use then: a default with `??`, or a branch with `if let`.

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let c = 'a'
    print(c + 1)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let c = 'a'
    print(char(i64(c) + 1) ?? c)
}
```
explanations.E0139:
# E0139: operator on a value of a type parameter

An operator on a value of a type parameter `T`, or of a type that holds one, can need a bound. This error is for a comparison that a bound on `T` can give. It is also for the arithmetic operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%`, and for a unary `-`, which no bound gives. `Eq` gives `==` and `!=` on `T`, and on an array, an optional or an enum that holds a `T`, as `[T]` does. `Ord` gives `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` on `T` itself. A `contains` on a `[T]` is [E0154](E0154.md), not this error: the prelude writes it for an element that conforms to `Eq`.

A bound on `T` cannot fix a part that fails by itself. An example is an enum with a `T` and a `Node` that has no `Eq`. That error is [E0159](E0159.md), whatever the order of the parts.

A type can write a conformance whose bound a bound on `T` meets. With `extend<A: Eq> Pair<A>: Eq`, `x == x` on a `Pair<T>` is this error, and the help is to bound `T`: `add a bound: T: Eq`. When the bounds that fail need different changes, the error is [E0159](E0159.md), with a label on the first bound that fails and no help.

Comparing an optional with `None` is allowed: on a `T?` or a `[T]?`, `x == None` and `x != None` test only whether a value is there, and need nothing from `T`. Comparing the values inside, as `x == y` on two `T?` does, needs `T: Eq`.

## Why

`T` may stand for any type, and not every type has every operator: a class has no `<`, and an array has no `+`. A bound says that a type conforms to an interface, and the interfaces `Eq` and `Ord` give the operators. A generic function can use only what its bounds give.

Operands of different types are the mistake, whatever bounds the types have. That error is [E0047](E0047.md) for `==` and `!=`, and [E0032](E0032.md) for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `contains`. An operand that cannot be the type of the other one has the same rule. A number that does not fit is [E0040](E0040.md), [E0042](E0042.md) or [E0104](E0104.md). This error comes when the operands are one type. A `T` beside a `T?` counts as one type. So does an operand whose own error leaves it with no type. An error in an operand that is not about its type, as a wrong `let` in a block, does not hide this error. When this error comes, the help shows the bound to add. It keeps the bounds that `T` has: `T: Display` gets `T: Display & Ord`. The help names a type parameter only. A class `Box<T>` has no `==` of its own, so a bound on `T` does not give one: that is [E0159](E0159.md), and `Box<T>` must conform to `Eq`. The same holds for any other part of the operand that is not a type parameter. A comparison that the type does not have for any `T` is not this error. It is [E0159](E0159.md). For example, `<` on a `[T]`, a `T?` or a `Result<T, i64>` is E0159, because an array, an optional and a `Result` have no `<`, and no bound on `T` gives one.

## Broken

```sisu
fn smaller<T>(a: T, b: T) -> bool {
    a < b
}

fn main() {}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn smaller<T: Ord>(a: T, b: T) -> bool {
    a < b
}

fn main() {
    print(smaller(1, 2))
}
```
